```{r}
# Install required packages if not already installed
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidytext", "janeaustenr"))

# Load the libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(janeaustenr)

# Note: No print statement is needed; successful loading is indicated by the absence of error messages.
```

```{r}
# Load the text of "Pride and Prejudice" from the janeaustenr package
# The text is stored as a character vector where each element is a line of the book
austen_books <- tibble(text = prideprejudice) %>%
  mutate(line = row_number()) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

# Display the first 10 rows to verify the tidy data structure
head(austen_books, 10)
```
```{r}
# Load the standard stop words dataset provided by tidytext
data(stop_words)

# Filter out stop words and count the frequency of remaining words
top_words <- austen_books %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# Display the top 20 most frequent content words
head(top_words, 20)
```
```{r}
# Generate a horizontal bar chart for the top 15 words
top_words %>%
  top_n(15) %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = word, y = n, fill = word)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 15 Most Frequent Content Words in Pride and Prejudice",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 12))
```
Linguistic Observations: The frequency distribution highlights the narrative focus of the novel. Words like "elizabeth", "darcy", "miss", and "time" dominate the text, reflecting the character-driven and social nature of Austen's writing.
